sources.citation: OLAC combined catalog, 'OLAC resources in and about the Ngwaba language' (Internet Archive copy, up-to-date as of 15 Aug 2024).
sources.note: Only two records: the Glottolog languoid page and the Ethnologue entry. No archived wordlist, recordings, grammar or phonology for ngw in any OLAC archive.

sources.citation: Newman, Paul (comp.). 2022. Comprehensive Bibliography of Chadic and Hausa Linguistics, Fifth Edition. Bloomington: Indiana University, IUScholarWorks (electronic publication, hdl 2022/27402, DOI 10.5967/5q3g-t220).
sources.note: Nothing: listed as NEGATIVE EVIDENCE only. The exhaustive Chadic field bibliography (5th ed., 2022; every entry keyworded by language, e.g. '[Kw: CB C-C Bata]') contains no entry keyworded Ngwaba, Gombi or Goba and the string 'Ngwaba' occurs nowhere in it; the Kraft 1981 Chadic Wordlists entry's language keywords (..Gude Gudu Guduf Higi Hona Jilbu Kapsiki Kilba Mandara/Wandala Margi Mafa/Matakam Nzanyi Putai Tera..) confirm Kraft holds no Ngwaba list.

sources.citation: Harley, Matthew. 2021. Nominal and verbal plurality in the Mandara and Ɓata subgroups of Central Chadic. Afrika und Übersee 94: 91-126. DOI 10.15460/auue.2021.94.1.223 (open access).
sources.note: Nothing on Ngwaba. General remark only that in the Ɓata subgroup /ə/ is typically phonemic and interacts with palatalised/labialised consonants; data are from Nzanyi, Ɓacama, Glavda, Guduf etc.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2019 [file dated Sept 2020]. An Atlas of Nigerian Languages, Edition IV. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. Entry '343. Ngwaba', printed p. 75 (p. 103).
sources.note: Nothing. The entry gives only: alternate names Gombi, Goba; Adamawa State, Gombi LGA at Fachi and Gudumiya; 'less than 1000' speakers; 'Chadic: Biu-Mandara sub-branch A: Bata group'; 'Source(s) Blench (1987)' (the Atlas defines Source(s) as the author's own field visit or personal communication). No Refs line at all: no wordlist, phonology, grammar or dictionary is listed, whereas neighbouring entries carry 'Wordlist: Kraft (1981)' etc. The Atlas's classification index (p. ~ 'Biu-Mandara / Tera group') lists Ngwaba under Tera, not Bata.

sources.citation: Ngwaba project (translators) / Nigeria Bible Translation Trust (NBTT, Door43 organisation 'NBTT'; two books also under user 'Bayan'). 2019. Ngwaba New Testament [27 books, resource type 'REG'], translationStudio text projects ngw_mat.. ngw_rev_text_reg, released on Door43 6 Aug - 23 Oct 2019, source text English ULB v6. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. Listed by find.bible as 'Ngwaba New Testament, 2019' (id NGWUFW).
sources.note: No linguistic content at all: it is running Scripture text. The practical orthography used marks neither tone nor stress (sample, Mark 1:9: 'kǝr tsagi Yesu mashi made'a dǝ Nazaratsǝ Galili, kǝr Yahya ǝsa babtismatsǝ yawa mobera Urdun'); vowels a e i o u ǝ, consonant digraphs tl, gh, sh, zh, ts, dz, implosives ɓ ɗ, apostrophe. Useful as the first sizeable open corpus of Ngwaba (c. 8,000 verses) for any future phonological work, but it states nothing about prosody.

sources.citation: Gravina, Richard. 2014. The Phonology of Proto-Central Chadic: the reconstruction of the phonology and lexicon of Proto-Central Chadic, and the linguistic history of the Central Chadic languages. Utrecht: LOT (LOT 375).
sources.note: Nothing about Ngwaba stress. Table 3 'Lexical data sources' (p. 16) reads 'Ngwaba [ngw] Bata none', i.e. Gravina had no Ngwaba data; the reconstruction explicitly excludes 'tone or stress'. Ngwaba is only named as one of the twelve Bata-group languages (pp. 27, 47-48, 3.3.1).

sources.citation: Newman, Paul. 2013. The Chadic Language Family: Classification and Name Index. Mega-Chad Research Network, Miscellaneous electronic publications (IUScholarWorks copy, hdl 2022/20964; CC BY-NC). 11 pp.
sources.note: classification and name index only; no linguistic data; nothing on stress or tone

sources.citation: Brenzinger, Matthias (ed.). 2007. Language Diversity Endangered. (Trends in Linguistics. Studies and Monographs 181.) Berlin / New York: Mouton de Gruyter. xvii+454 pp. [copies we hold is the complete volume; African chapters read: ch. 6 Brenzinger 'Language Endangerment in Northern Africa' 123–139; ch. 7 Blench 'Endangered Languages in West Africa' 140–162; ch. 8 Connell 'Endangered Languages in Central Africa' 163–178; ch. 9 Brenzinger 'Language Endangerment in Southern and Eastern Africa' 179–204]
sources.note: Nothing on stress/tone: table row only — 'Two villages in 1991'.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. [2006, circulation draft]. Classification of Afroasiatic (AALIST). 15 pp.
sources.note: Nothing; Ngwaba appears only as a name in the Central Chadic, Tera group list (p. 6).

sources.citation: Ethnologue, 14th (2000), 15th (2005) and 16th (2009) edition entries for Ngwaba [ngw], read through the the Internet Archive.
sources.note: Nothing linguistic beyond classification 'Afro-Asiatic, Chadic, Biu-Mandara, A, A.8'; population 10,000 (1993 CAPRO); Gombi LGA at Fachi and Guduniya, and Hong LGA, 2 villages; 14th ed.: 'Investigation needed: intelligibility with Nzanyi'.

sources.citation: Endangered Languages Project, page for Ngwaba [ngw] (Internet Archive copy).
sources.note: Nothing; its four sources are Ethnologue 16 (2009), UNESCO Atlas (Moseley 2010), the World Oral Literature Project, and Fakuade, Gambo & Bashir 2003 (a language-shift questionnaire survey: 33% of Ngwaba respondents use Ngwaba with parents/children).

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x, languoid page ngwa1251 (Ngwaba).
sources.note: No descriptive reference at all: only Gravina 2014 pp. 47-48 and Barreteau & Dieu 2000 pp. 65-66 (classification comments), Campbell et al. 2022 and Lewis 2009 (endangerment). Alternate names Goba, Gombi, Enguaba.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Ngwaba language' and 'Biu-Mandara languages' (en), 'Ngwaba jezik' (hr).
sources.note: Nothing; stubs citing only Ethnologue and Blench 2006. The Biu-Mandara page notes Ngwaba is placed in Bata (A.8) by some and in Tera (A.1) by Blench.

sources.citation: Fakuade, Gbenga, Matudi Gambo & Abdullahi Bashir. 2003. Language shift from mother tongues towards Fulfulde in Adamawa State, Nigeria: causes and consequences. Anthropological Linguistics 45(3): 296-315.
